newsitem.title: USA: Former N.Y. Blood Center worker arrested.
newsitem.headline: Former N.Y. Blood Center worker arrested.

text.p: A former assistant manager in the viral testing laboratory of the New York Blood Centre, the nation's biggest independent supplier of blood, was arrested on Monday for allegedly manipulating testing for viruses such as HIV and hepatitis.
Eliazar Maniago, 36, of Bergenfield, New Jersey, was charged in a criminal complaint filed by prosecutors in Manhattan federal court.

The New York Blood Centre (NYBC) provides 80 percent of the blood supply in the New York area. It also provides blood donor testing services for facilities located in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Tennessee and imports and exports blood products to and from Europe.
The complaint alleges that from 1993 to about November 1966 Maniago manipulated the testing of blood for such viruses as HIV, which causes AIDS, and hepatitis.
A special agent for the Food and Drug Administration said in the complaint that an FDA expert had advised that the alleged manipulations undermine the reliability of the blood tests.
If convicted, Maniago faces a maximum sentence of three years in jail and a $10,000 fine.
In December, prosecutors filed a civil suit against the NYBC for failing to maintain adequate methods of screening blood for infection.

Federal prosecutors simultaneously announced they had also filed a consent decree in which the centre agreed to correct violations and take steps to assure the purity and quality of its blood products.

The civil lawsuit provided a long list of violations including that the centre did not follow standards designed to prevent the introduction, transmission or spread of communicable diseases including the HIV virus.
The FDA, which conducted inspections in 1994 and 1995 of NYBC's two locations in Manhattan, raised questions about the tests it used to screen blood.

It found that the centre used improper testing practices, failed to maintain complete and adequate operating procedures; maintained inaccurate recordkeeping, provided inadequate personnel training and had inadequate security controls of computerized operations to ensure the integrity of the data.
The FDA notified the NYBC of its findings and issued a warning letter in March 1995.
